source.title: What Matters for Grocery Product Retrieval with Open Source Vision Language Models
source.authors: Emmanuel G. Maminta; Rowel O. Atienza

record.file_problem: The text includes a “[truncated for brevity]” marker in Section 4.1; the rest of the supplied paper is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream retrieval performance of pretrained vision-language models at different parameter counts, but does not measure language-model held-out loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports retrieval scores and comparisons, not power-law fits or extrapolations. Its comparisons across checkpoints vary architecture and often pretraining data as well as size, so they do not isolate a parameter-scaling relationship. The data-quality and resolution findings do not directly test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a zero-shot benchmark of 190 off-the-shelf OpenCLIP vision-language checkpoints on grocery retrieval. It fits no scaling law. It measures no pretraining loss. It runs no controlled sweep over parameters, tokens or compute. Size comparisons across checkpoints also vary architecture, pretraining data and resolution. The 'data quality trumps scale' argument concerns heterogeneous checkpoints, not a scaling relationship with other factors held fixed. So the results do not bear on whether any version holds; the paper only discusses scale in that framing.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude that pretraining-data quality, not parameter count, sets the zero-shot grocery retrieval ceiling (up to 16.6% gains). They find compact clean-data models such as MobileCLIP-B (150M) beat noisier 351M models. They report a 17.5% Recall@5-to-Recall@1 gap showing poor SKU-level ranking. They also recommend MobileCLIP-B for edge and PE-Core-L-14 for server deployment, and 384px as a practical resolution ceiling.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates pretrained vision-language checkpoints on zero-shot grocery retrieval; it does not measure language-model pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported retrieval performance varies with pretraining data and image resolution; the paper also reports that different model families and sizes perform differently.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing only the pretraining data source changes Recall@1 substantially. For the same backbone, DataComp-XL beats LAION-2B, which beats WIT-400M, by up to +16.6% (Table 4). Small uncurated datasets such as YFCC-15M and CommonPool-S cause drops of 93–97% (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Zero-shot downstream retrieval of contrastive VLMs depends strongly on pretraining-data quality and scale, with effects comparable to or exceeding a ~3x parameter increase.

fits_no_version.finding: On noisy CommonPool data, ViT-B-32 (151M) falls 79.4% relative to WIT-400M, while ViT-L-14 (428M) gains 1.0% (Table 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger contrastive VLMs are more robust to noisy pretraining data than smaller ones.

record.problems: The evaluation is limited to GroceryVision and 409 SKUs. Checkpoint comparisons generally vary architecture, pretraining data, and resolution as well as parameter count, so they do not isolate a scaling effect. The text reports uncertainty only for repeated forward passes, not for most comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the data-source comparisons in Tables 4–7: those results concern data filtration and data scale rather than the parameter- or loss-based downstream predictability measured for V6. The paper reports no language-model loss, power-law fits, or compute-optimal allocation results.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, data or compute.
No power-law form is fitted for vision-language models; it only evaluates released checkpoints.
Gives no fit of downstream performance against scale or pretraining loss. Size comparisons are uncontrolled across data and architecture.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice comparisons.

missing.what: Same-data size comparisons within the ViT family. ViT-B-32 (151M) vs ViT-L-14 (428M) scores 0.403→0.568 on WIT-400M, 0.481→0.619 on LAION-2B and 0.521→0.693 on DataComp-XL. These are only two-size, uncontrolled-architecture points with no fit.
missing.versions: none directly. They would matter only if V5/V6 were extended to downstream scores of VLM checkpoints.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V6 limits_scope label are not justified. Checkpoint comparisons do not isolate scale, and V6 concerns predictable improvement with scale, which this benchmark does not fit or control. Rows T1-8 and T1-9 duplicate T1-2 and T1-1. The text has a truncation marker in Section 4.1 that does not affect results.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fit or prediction of much larger runs is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
No comparison holds parameter count fixed while varying depth, width, or other architecture details.
The study evaluates vision-language models on retrieval, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in another modality or training regime.
No pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance prediction is tested; checkpoint comparisons are not controlled sweeps over size, and only grocery retrieval is evaluated.
The paper does not test fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or departures from fitted power laws.
